title: Abdominal Pain
hpi_narrative: {{patient_name}} is a man who recently returned from a cruise ship and presents with abdominal pain, nausea, vomiting, jaundice, and shortness of breath. He has RUQ tenderness on exam. LFTs are markedly elevated in the 2000-3000 range. The cruise ship travel and profoundly elevated transaminases are highly suspicious for acute viral hepatitis A (fecal-oral transmission). His episodes of vomiting led to aspiration pneumonia. Acetaminophen level should be checked to rule out overdose as a cause of acute liver injury. Management is supportive: IV fluids, antiemetics, oxygen for hypoxia, and antibiotics for aspiration pneumonia per ATS/IDSA guidelines (treat as community-acquired pneumonia; no anaerobic coverage needed without abscess/empyema). Acetaminophen is contraindicated with hepatic injury. Admit to inpatient unit.

teach_me_steps.reasoning: Cruise ship = HAV risk (fecal-oral). High LFTs + jaundice = acute hepatitis. Always rule out acetaminophen toxicity in acute liver injury.

teach_me_steps.order: Treat aspiration pneumonia per CAP guidelines
teach_me_steps.reasoning: ATS/IDSA: aspiration pneumonia = CAP treatment. No anaerobic coverage needed unless abscess/empyema. Levofloxacin, ceftriaxone + azithromycin.

teach_me_steps.order: Supportive care: IV fluids + antiemetics + O2
teach_me_steps.reasoning: HAV is self-limited. Supportive care while liver recovers. Avoid hepatotoxins (acetaminophen, alcohol).
LFTs 2000-3000, jaundiced, intractable vomiting — requires IV fluids, IV antibiotics, LFT monitoring.

case_summary: Hepatitis A from cruise ship (fecal-oral) with aspiration pneumonia from vomiting. LFTs 2000-3000. Supportive care + CAP antibiotics + O2. Avoid acetaminophen. Inpatient admission.
